To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Treg/HIV+, as compared with Treg from healthy individuals, exert a differential effect on CD8+ subsets, and maintain CD8+ T memory/effector balance, at least partially through the PD- 1/PD-L pathway.
Treg from patients infected by HIV exerted a defect on the differentiation and the exhaustion of HIV-Gag specific CD8+ T responses.

Treg/HIV+, unlike Treg/HIV, do not suppress polyclonal autlogous CD8 T cell function, but inhibit significantly CEF- but not Gag-specific CD 8 T cells, and do not inhibit the differentiation and the PD-1 expression of Gag-specific CD T cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of regulatory CD4+FoxP3+ (Treg) cells and their role in the control of HIV infection, in particular in the modulation of CD8+ T-cell responses and their exhaustion.
the role of Treg in HIV infection.
the mechanisms by which Treg regulate the differentiation and the effector functions of CD8+ T effector cells, and the consequences for the control of HIV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV infection is associated with a defective Treg function, at least in the context of CD8 T cells differentiation and PD-1/PDL-1 expression.
HIV infection is a complex disease, which involves multiple mechanisms and pathways.
the HIV infection has a significant effect on the Treg function and that this defect may contribute to the exhaustion or dysfunction of HIV-specific T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Treg from HIV-infected individuals have a defect in inhibiting both the differentiation and expression of PD- 1/PD-LI of HIV-specific CD8+T cells, which might contribute to the T cell exhaustion in HIV-infected individuals.

Treg from chronic HIV-infected patients have an intrinsic defect in the ability to suppress CD8 responses and to maintain the memory /effector CD8+T cells balance, at leas in part through the PDL1/PD-1 pathway.
Tregs are not able to control the HIV-specific T cells responses in chronic HIV infected patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of Treg are subset- and antigen-specific, suggesting that the Treg-mediated effects on HIV-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells are likely to be complex.
Treg are not only important in maintaining homeostatic CD8 T cell responses, but they also have a direct impact on HIV-specific responses.
Treg from chronically infected patients do not inhibit HIV-specific CD8+ cells.
